claim: Birds and mammals are the only true living endothermic vertebrates.
source: The only true living endothermic vertebrates are birds and mammals, which produce and regulate their internal temperature quite independently from their surroundings.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge about modern vertebrate physiology.

claim: Anatomical clues suggest that endothermy originated during the Permian or Triassic in mammal ancestors.
source: For mammal ancestors, anatomical clues suggest that endothermy originated during the Permian or Triassic.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior anatomical studies, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: Cynodonts and dicynodonts independently acquired constant elevated thermometabolism.
source: It is proposed that cynodonts and dicynodonts independently acquired constant elevated thermometabolism, respectively within the Eucynodontia and Lystrosauridae + Kannemeyeriiformes clades.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on oxygen isotope analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mammalian endothermy originated in the Epicynodontia during the middle-late Permian.
source: We conclude that mammalian endothermy originated in the Epicynodontia during the middle-late Permian.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the oxygen isotope data and phylogenetic analysis presented in the study.

claim: Major global climatic and environmental fluctuations were the most likely selective pressures on the success of elevated thermometabolism.
source: Major global climatic and environmental fluctuations were the most likely selective pressures on the success of such elevated thermometabolism.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on correlation between climate data and the timing of endothermy evolution.

claim: Endothermy is defined as the ability to actively produce body heat through metabolic activity.
source: This character is defined here as the ability to actively produce body heat through metabolic activity (Cannon and Nedergaard, 2004).
evidence: This definition is supported by a citation to Cannon and Nedergaard, 2004.

claim: Endothermic vertebrates are able to colonise environments with extreme thermal conditions by actively raising and maintaining body temperature.
source: By actively raising and maintaining body temperature within a narrow range that allows optimal physiological and biochemical functioning, endothermic vertebrates are able to colonise environments with extreme thermal conditions, for example freezing at high latitudes and altitudes (Day et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Day et al., 2015 and represents established knowledge about endothermy.

claim: Only birds and mammals fall within the endothermy end of the thermoregulatory spectrum amongst modern vertebrates.
source: Amongst modern vertebrates, various thermoregulatory strategies have been adopted between these two end-members, such as regional endothermy (Bernal et al., 2001; Katz, 2002) or inertial homeothermy (McNab and Auffenberg, 1976), and only birds and mammals fall within the endothermy end of the spectrum.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Bird thermoregulation originated within non-avian dinosaurs or earlier within basal archosauriforms.
source: It has been proposed that bird thermoregulation originated within non-avian dinosaurs (Seebacher, 2003; Amiot et al., 2006; Grady et al., 2014), or even earlier within basal archosauriforms (Farmer and Carrier, 2000; de Ricqlès et al., 2003; Seymour et al., 2004; Summers, 2005; Gower et al., 2014; Legendre et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The oldest synapsid fossils preserved with fur imprints are Castorocauda and Megaconus from the Middle-Late Jurassic of China.
source: The oldest synapsid fossils preserved with fur imprints are Castorocauda (Ji et al., 2006) and Megaconus (Zhou et al., 2013). These early relatives of mammals were recovered from the Middle-Late Jurassic of China, implying that hair and fur appeared before ~165 Ma.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ji et al., 2006 and Zhou et al., 2013.

claim: The occurrence of retracted, fully ossified and non-ramified infraorbital canals within non-mammaliaform Prozostrodontia implies an age of approximately 240 to 246 Ma for the occurrence of fur and hair.
source: The occurrence of retracted, fully ossified and non-ramified infraorbital canals (a structure associated with the presence of maxillary vibrissae) within non-mammaliaform Prozostrodontia, implies an older age of approximately 240 to 246 Ma for the occurrence of fur and hair (Benoit et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is based on anatomical inference supported by citation to Benoit et al., 2016b.

claim: A bony secondary palate is associated with efficient respiratory capabilities linked to high energy required for elevated metabolic rates.
source: Another anatomical character interpreted as associated with endothermy is the bony secondary palate. This is a feature associated with efficient respiratory capabilities considered to be linked to the high energy required for elevated metabolic rates.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on anatomical-functional relationships.

claim: A complete bony secondary palate is fully developed in some Triassic non-mammaliamorph therapsids, including bauriid therocephalians and cynodonts.
source: In some Triassic non-mammaliamorph therapsids, bauriid therocephalians and cynodonts, a bony secondary palate is fully developed (Abdala et al., 2014).
evidence: This anatomical observation is supported by citation to Abdala et al., 2014.

claim: A complete bony secondary palate is present in dicynodonts and is primarily formed by the premaxilla.
source: It is noteworthy that a complete bony secondary palate is also present in dicynodonts, however it is primarily formed by the premaxilla (King, 1988) and not the maxilla as documented in therocephalians, cynodonts and extant mammals.
evidence: This anatomical observation is supported by citation to King, 1988.

claim: A secondary osseous palate occurs in some ectotherms (crocodiles, scincid lizards), questioning its direct link to endothermy.
source: Although a secondary osseous palate is ubiquitous in mammals, it also occurs in a few ectotherms (crocodiles, scincid lizards), thus questioning its direct link to endothermy (Bennett and Ruben, 1986).
evidence: This comparative observation is supported by citation to Bennett and Ruben, 1986.

claim: Almost all extant endotherms possess nasal turbinate bones covered with mucosa that reduce heat loss and moisten air during respiration.
source: Almost all extant endotherms possess nasal turbinate bones covered with mucosa that reduce heat loss and moisten air during respiration (Owerkowicz et al., 2015).
evidence: This anatomical-functional observation is supported by citation to Owerkowicz et al., 2015.

claim: Nasal turbinates are absent in extant ectotherms.
source: This feature, absent in extant ectotherms (Witmer, 1995), may have been present in therocephalian, cynodont and dicynodont therapsids, as postulated from bony ridges in the nasal cavities interpreted as supports for the turbinate complex (Hillenius, 1992, 1994; Crompton et al., 2017).
evidence: This comparative observation is supported by citation to Witmer, 1995.

claim: Nasal turbinates may have been present in therocephalian, cynodont and dicynodont therapsids based on bony ridges in the nasal cavities.
source: This feature, absent in extant ectotherms (Witmer, 1995), may have been present in therocephalian, cynodont and dicynodont therapsids, as postulated from bony ridges in the nasal cavities interpreted as supports for the turbinate complex (Hillenius, 1992, 1994; Crompton et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on anatomical evidence, supported by citations.

claim: Fibrolamellar bone (FLB) is associated with highly vascularised woven-fibred matrix and primary osteons and is often used as evidence of high metabolic activity.
source: A peculiar histological structure of fast-growing bone associated with highly vascularised woven-fibred matrix and primary osteons known as fibrolamellar bone (FLB), is another feature often used as evidence of a high metabolic activity (Montes et al., 2010; Legendre et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Montes et al., 2010 and Legendre et al., 2016.

claim: FLB has been found in some therapsid genera including Aelurognathus, Pristerognathus, Tritylodon, Oudenodon, Lystrosaurus, and Moghreberia.
source: Ray et al. (2004) and Olivier et al. (2017) analysed several therapsid groups (anomodont, gorgonopsian, therocephalian, cynodont) and found FLB in some genera (Aelurognathus, Pristerognathus, Tritylodon, Oudenodon, Lystrosaurus, Moghreberia), suggesting sustained fast growth, and thus elevated metabolic activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ray et al., 2004 and Olivier et al., 2017.

claim: The presence of FLB in some therapsids suggests sustained fast growth and elevated metabolic activity.
source: Ray et al. (2004) and Olivier et al. (2017) analysed several therapsid groups (anomodont, gorgonopsian, therocephalian, cynodont) and found FLB in some genera (Aelurognathus, Pristerognathus, Tritylodon, Oudenodon, Lystrosaurus, Moghreberia), suggesting sustained fast growth, and thus elevated metabolic activity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from histological data cited from Ray et al., 2004 and Olivier et al., 2017.

claim: FLB has been demonstrated in some earlier non-therapsid synapsids such as Sphenacodon, Dimetrodon and Ophiacodon.
source: The presence of FLB has also been demonstrated in some earlier non-therapsid synapsids such as Sphenacodon, Dimetrodon or even Ophiacodon (Huttenlocker et al., 2010; Shelton et al., 2012; Shelton and Sander, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Huttenlocker et al., 2010; Shelton et al., 2012; Shelton and Sander, 2017.

claim: FLB occurs in some ectotherms such as some turtles and crocodilians.
source: However, FLB also occurs in a few ectotherms such as in some turtles and crocodilians, and is absent in small mammals and passerine birds (Bouvier, 1977), showing that FLB is mostly correlated with high growth rates, which does not always correlate to high metabolic rates.
evidence: This comparative observation is supported by citation to Bouvier, 1977.

claim: FLB is absent in small mammals and passerine birds.
source: However, FLB also occurs in a few ectotherms such as in some turtles and crocodilians, and is absent in small mammals and passerine birds (Bouvier, 1977), showing that FLB is mostly correlated with high growth rates, which does not always correlate to high metabolic rates.
evidence: This observation is supported by citation to Bouvier, 1977.

claim: FLB is mostly correlated with high growth rates, which does not always correlate to high metabolic rates.
source: However, FLB also occurs in a few ectotherms such as in some turtles and crocodilians, and is absent in small mammals and passerine birds (Bouvier, 1977), showing that FLB is mostly correlated with high growth rates, which does not always correlate to high metabolic rates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparative observations cited from Bouvier, 1977.

claim: The oxygen isotope fractionation between bone or tooth phosphate and body fluids is temperature dependent.
source: Because the oxygen isotope fractionation between bone or tooth phosphate and body fluids is temperature dependent, and phosphate has a strong resistance to diagenetic alteration, oxygen isotope compositions of therapsid apatite phosphate (δ18Op) has been used in this pilot study to investigate the origin of mammalian endothermy.
evidence: This is established knowledge in isotope geochemistry.

claim: Phosphate has a strong resistance to diagenetic alteration.
source: Because the oxygen isotope fractionation between bone or tooth phosphate and body fluids is temperature dependent, and phosphate has a strong resistance to diagenetic alteration, oxygen isotope compositions of therapsid apatite phosphate (δ18Op) has been used in this pilot study to investigate the origin of mammalian endothermy.
evidence: This is established knowledge in isotope geochemistry and taphonomy.

claim: The δ18Op value of vertebrate apatite reflects both the oxygen isotope composition of the animal body water and its body temperature.
source: Indeed the δ18Op value of vertebrate apatite (bone, tooth) reflects both the oxygen isotope composition of the animal body water (δ18Obw) and its body temperature (Tb).
evidence: This is established knowledge in isotope geochemistry applied to paleobiology.

claim: Body water derives mainly from drinking meteoric water or plant water.
source: Body water derives mainly from drinking meteoric water or plant water (D'Angela and Longinelli, 1990; Kohn, 1996a), and the δ18O value of this water in turn depends on climatic parameters such as air temperature, hygrometry, and amount of precipitation (Dansgaard, 1964; von Grafenstein et al., 1996; Fricke and O'Neil, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to D'Angela and Longinelli, 1990 and Kohn, 1996a.

claim: The δ18O value of body water depends on climatic parameters such as air temperature, hygrometry, and amount of precipitation.
source: Body water derives mainly from drinking meteoric water or plant water (D'Angela and Longinelli, 1990; Kohn, 1996a), and the δ18O value of this water in turn depends on climatic parameters such as air temperature, hygrometry, and amount of precipitation (Dansgaard, 1964; von Grafenstein et al., 1996; Fricke and O'Neil, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dansgaard, 1964; von Grafenstein et al., 1996; Fricke and O'Neil, 1999.

claim: Variations in the δ18O values of ectotherm apatite along with increasing latitude are expected to reflect decreasing air temperatures.
source: Variations in the δ18O values of ectotherm apatite, along with increasing latitude, are expected to reflect decreasing air temperatures as their body temperatures follow those of the environment.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the relationship between ectotherm body temperature and environmental temperature.

claim: Endotherms with constant body temperature should not be affected by environmental temperature changes.
source: In contrast endotherms, which have a constant body temperature, should not be affected by environmental temperatures changes.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the definition of endothermy.

claim: Physiological adaptation to specific habitat use affects the δ18Obw value by controlling the magnitude of body input and output oxygen fluxes.
source: Moreover, physiological adaptation to specific habitat use (aquatic, semi-aquatic or terrestrial) affects the δ18Obw value by controlling the magnitude of body input and output oxygen fluxes, some of them being associated with oxygen isotopic fractionations (Amiot et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Amiot et al., 2010.

claim: Co-existing endotherms and ectotherms should have distinct apatite δ18Op values reflecting their body temperature and ecological differences.
source: Therefore, co-existing endotherms and ectotherms should have distinct apatite δ18Op values reflecting their body temperature and ecological differences.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the principles of oxygen isotope fractionation and thermoregulation.

claim: By comparing apatite δ18Op values of therapsids with those of co-existing ectotherms of known ecologies at various palaeolatitudes, it should be possible to infer therapsid thermophysiology.
source: By comparing apatite δ18Op values of therapsids with those of co-existing ectotherms of known ecologies at various palaeolatitudes, it should be possible to infer therapsid thermophysiology, a methodology that has previously been applied to non-avian dinosaurs (Fricke and Rogers, 2000; Amiot et al., 2006).
evidence: This methodological approach is supported by citations to Fricke and Rogers, 2000 and Amiot et al., 2006.

claim: The 13 sampled South African Permian therapsids come from three different assemblage zones of the Beaufort Group: the lower Tapinocephalus AZ, the Tropidostoma AZ and the lower Daptocephalus AZ.
source: The 13 sampled South African Permian therapsids come from three different assemblage zones (AZ) of the Beaufort Group: the lower Tapinocephalus AZ, the Tropidostoma AZ and the lower Daptocephalus AZ (Viglietti et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the sample collection supported by citation to Viglietti et al., 2016.

claim: δ18Op values of Dicynodon, Diictodon and Oudenodon are compared to those of the supposedly semi-aquatic parareptile Pareiasaurus.
source: In addition, δ18Op values of the therapsids Dicynodon, Diictodon and Oudenodon are compared to those of the supposedly semi-aquatic parareptile Pareiasaurus (Ivakhnenko, 2001; Kriloff et al., 2008) (see Appendix 1), with an observed range of +4.3 ± 0.4‰ to +6.8 ± 0.5‰ (Figure 1A) which is similar to that measured between therapsids and amphibians.
evidence: This comparison is based on isotope data presented in the study and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The δ18Op value range between Dicynodon, Diictodon, Oudenodon and Pareiasaurus (+4.3 ± 0.4‰ to +6.8 ± 0.5‰) supports the ectothermic status of these therapsids.
source: In addition, δ18Op values of the therapsids Dicynodon, Diictodon and Oudenodon are compared to those of the supposedly semi-aquatic parareptile Pareiasaurus (Ivakhnenko, 2001; Kriloff et al., 2008) (see Appendix 1), with an observed range of +4.3 ± 0.4‰ to +6.8 ± 0.5‰ (Figure 1A) which is similar to that measured between therapsids and amphibians. This also supports the ectothermic status of Dicynodon, Diictodon and Oudenodon.
evidence: This interpretation is based on isotope data shown in Figure 1A and comparison with theoretical predictions.

claim: Anteosaurus, Criocephalosaurus, Struthiocephalus, Glanosuchus and a titanosuchid from the lower Tapinocephalus AZ have δ18Op differences ranging from −1.4 ± 0.6‰ to 0.7 ± 1.0‰ compared to co-occurring basal pareiasaurs.
source: Anteosaurus, Criocephalosaurus, Struthiocephalus, Glanosuchus and a titanosuchid from the lower Tapinocephalus AZ have also been compared to two co-occuring basal pareiasaurs which are attributed to either Embrithosaurus, Nochelosaurus or Bradysaurus (Lee, 1997) and are considered to have been terrestrial animals (Canoville et al., 2014). From Figure 1B, the δ18Op differences range from −1.4 ± 0.6‰ to 0.7 ± 1.0‰, also supporting the ectothermic status of these therapsids.
evidence: This is based on isotope data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: The δ18Op differences between Anteosaurus, Criocephalosaurus, Struthiocephalus, Glanosuchus, a titanosuchid and co-occurring pareiasaurs support the ectothermic status of these therapsids.
source: From Figure 1B, the δ18Op differences range from −1.4 ± 0.6‰ to 0.7 ± 1.0‰, also supporting the ectothermic status of these therapsids.
evidence: This interpretation is based on isotope data shown in Figure 1B and comparison with theoretical predictions.

claim: The anteosaurid Sinophoneus yumenensis from the Middle Permian of China has a δ18Op value 4.4 ± 0.3‰ lower than the co-existing bolosaurid parareptile Belebey chengi.
source: From the Middle Permian of China, one anteosaurid Sinophoneus yumenensis from the low palaeolatitude locality of Dashankou has a δ18Op value 4.4 ± 0.3‰ lower than the co-existing bolosaurid parareptile Belebey chengi, which is considered to have been a terrestrial ectotherm (Berman et al., 2000; Müller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on isotope data from the study.

claim: The δ18Op difference between Sinophoneus and Belebey chengi is close to the expected ranges for ectothermic therapsids.
source: This difference between only two values would suggest that Sinophoneus was endothermic, but it is also very close to the expected ranges for ectothermic therapsids (Figure 1B).
evidence: This interpretation is based on comparison of data with theoretical predictions shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Considering Sinophoneus as semi-aquatic, the δ18Op difference would imply an ectothermic thermophysiology for this therapsid.
source: Considering Sinophoneus as semi-aquatic, as has been suggested for some anteosaurids (Boonstra, 1955, Boonstra, 1962), the δ18Op difference would imply an ectothermic thermophysiology for this therapsid.
evidence: This is an inference based on ecological assumptions and isotope data.

claim: Five Lystrosaurus specimens from the lower Lystrosaurus AZ have δ18Op values similar to those of the co-existing semi-aquatic stereospondyl Lydekkerina.
source: Also from South Africa, five Lystrosaurus specimens from the lower Lystrosaurus AZ have δ18Op values similar to those of the co-existing semi-aquatic stereospondyl Lydekkerina (Schoch, 2008; Canoville and Chinsamy, 2015).
evidence: This is based on isotope data from the study.

claim: An indeterminate lystrosaurid from the Induan Jiucaiyuan Formation has a δ18Op value similar (difference of −0.1 ± 0.6‰) to that of the proterosuchid 'Chasmatosaurus' yuani.
source: In addition, an indeterminate lystrosaurid from the Induan Jiucaiyuan Formation of the Xinjiang Province has a δ18Op value similar (with a difference of −0.1 ± 0.6‰; Figure 2B) to that of the proterosuchid 'Chasmatosaurus' yuani, a basal archosauriform considered terrestrial and possessing an intermediate thermometabolsim based on a palaeohistological study (Botha-Brink and Smith, 2011).
evidence: This is based on isotope data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The combined results from South Africa and China suggest that the analysed lystrosaurids were terrestrial endotherms.
source: The combined results from South Africa and China suggest that the analysed lystrosaurids were terrestrial endotherms (Figure 2; see Appendix 1).
evidence: This interpretation is based on isotope data shown in Figure 2 and comparison with theoretical predictions.

claim: Shansiodon wangi and Parakannemeyeria youngi from the Ermaying Formation have δ18Op values of 2.0 ± 0.7‰ and 1.7 ± 0.7‰ respectively, both lower than the sampled erythrosuchid archosauriform Shansisuchus shansisuchus.
source: From the Ermaying Formation of the Shanxi Province (China), the therapsids Shansiodon wangi and Parakannemeyeria youngi have respectively δ18Op values of 2.0 ± 0.7‰ and 1.7 ± 0.7‰. These are both lower than the sampled erythrosuchid archosauriform Shansisuchus shansisuchus, which fall within two theoretical overlapping ranges (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on isotope data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: If Shansisuchus is considered a terrestrial endotherm-like animal, then Shansiodon wangi and Parakannemeyeria youngi also fall within the range of endotherms.
source: As for the South African erythrosuchids, if we consider Shansisuchus as a terrestrial endotherm-like animal and the low palaeolatitude of this part of China region, then the two therapsids also fall within the range of endotherms.
evidence: This is an inference based on isotope data and ecological assumptions.

claim: The late Anisian cynodont Diademodon has a δ18Op value 2.3 ± 0.5‰ higher than the co-existing aquatic stereospondyl Xenotosuchus africanus.
source: The late Anisian cynodont Diademodon has a δ18Op value 2.3 ± 0.5‰ higher than the co-existing aquatic stereospondyl Xenotosuchus africanus (Figure 3A), which is consistent with an endothermic status for Diademodon.
evidence: This is based on isotope data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The δ18Op difference between Diademodon and Xenotosuchus africanus is consistent with an endothermic status for Diademodon.
source: The late Anisian cynodont Diademodon has a δ18Op value 2.3 ± 0.5‰ higher than the co-existing aquatic stereospondyl Xenotosuchus africanus (Figure 3A), which is consistent with an endothermic status for Diademodon.
evidence: This interpretation is based on isotope data shown in Figure 3A and comparison with theoretical predictions.

claim: The Moroccan kannemeyeriiform Moghreberia nmachouensis from the early middle Carnian has a mean δ18Op value 2.0 ± 0.5‰ higher than the co-existing aquatic stereospondyl Almasaurus habbazi.
source: The Moroccan kannemeyeriiform Moghreberia nmachouensis from the early middle Carnian of the Argana Basin has a mean δ18Op value 2.0 ± 0.5‰ higher than the co-existing aquatic stereospondyl Almasaurus habbazi (Figure 3A), thus implying that Moghreberia nmachouensis was also endothermic.
evidence: This is based on isotope data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The δ18Op difference between Moghreberia nmachouensis and Almasaurus habbazi implies that Moghreberia nmachouensis was endothermic.
source: The Moroccan kannemeyeriiform Moghreberia nmachouensis from the early middle Carnian of the Argana Basin has a mean δ18Op value 2.0 ± 0.5‰ higher than the co-existing aquatic stereospondyl Almasaurus habbazi (Figure 3A), thus implying that Moghreberia nmachouensis was also endothermic.
evidence: This interpretation is based on isotope data shown in Figure 3A and comparison with theoretical predictions.

claim: An indeterminate cynodont from the Rhaetian Lower Elliot Formation has a δ18Op value 2.1 ± 0.3‰ higher than that of an indeterminate basal sauropodomorph.
source: An indeterminate cynodont from the Rhaetian Lower Elliot Formation of Lesotho has a δ18Op value 2.1 ± 0.3‰, higher than that of an indeterminate basal sauropodomorph.
evidence: This is based on isotope data from the study.

claim: The suspected endothermy and terrestriality of both dinosaurs and cynodonts are in agreement with their δ18Op difference that falls within the expected range predicting similar thermophysiology.
source: The suspected endothermy and terrestriality of both dinosaurs (Amiot et al., 2006; D'Emic, 2015) and cynodonts are in agreement with their δ18Op difference that falls within the expected range predicting similar thermophysiology between the two (Figure 3B).
evidence: This interpretation is based on isotope data shown in Figure 3B, comparison with theoretical predictions, and citations.

claim: Six of the interpreted endothermic therapsids belong to the L+K clade: Moghreberia nmachouensis, Parakannemeyeria youngi, Kannemeyeria simocephalus, Shansiodon wangi, Lystrosaurus, and an indeterminate lystrosaurid.
source: Among the interpreted endothermic therapsids, six belong to the L+K clade (Figure 4): Moghreberia nmachouensis, Parakannemeyeria youngi, Kannemeyeria simocephalus and Shansiodon wangi belong to the Kannemeyeriiformes clade, whereas the Lystrosauridae clade comprises Lystrosaurus and the Chinese indeterminate lystrosaurid.
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic relationships shown in Figure 4 and the isotope interpretations.

claim: The interpretation of L+K clade taxa as endothermic-like animals is better supported for the African Kannemeyeriiformes than for the Chinese species.
source: The interpretation of these taxa as endothermic-like animals is better supported for the African Kannemeyeriiformes, M. nmachouensis and K. simocephalus, where more individuals were sampled, than for the Chinese species, S. wangi and P. youngi.
evidence: This is an assessment of the strength of evidence based on sample size.

claim: Viglietti et al. (2013) demonstrated aggregating behaviour in the Early Triassic L. declivis and interpreted this as a means to keep warm under extreme climatic conditions.
source: Concerning the lystrosaurids, Viglietti et al. (2013) demonstrated aggregating behaviour in the Early Triassic L. declivis and interpreted this as a means to keep warm under extreme climatic conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Viglietti et al., 2013.

claim: The aggregating behaviour interpretation for Lystrosaurus is in agreement with the endothermic interpretation from isotope data.
source: Concerning the lystrosaurids, Viglietti et al. (2013) demonstrated aggregating behaviour in the Early Triassic L. declivis and interpreted this as a means to keep warm under extreme climatic conditions. This is in agreement with our endothermic interpretation for the genus.
evidence: This is an inference connecting behavioral evidence with isotope-based interpretation.

claim: Dicynodon seems to have been ectothermic based on isotope interpretations.
source: Based on the above interpretations, Dicynodon seems to have been ectothermic, a fact which would suggests the rise of endothermy amongst the dicynodont L+K clade during the latest Permian (Lopingian).
evidence: This interpretation is based on isotope data presented earlier in the manuscript.

claim: The rise of endothermy amongst the dicynodont L+K clade occurred during the latest Permian (Lopingian).
source: Based on the above interpretations, Dicynodon seems to have been ectothermic, a fact which would suggests the rise of endothermy amongst the dicynodont L+K clade during the latest Permian (Lopingian).
evidence: This is an inference based on isotope data and phylogenetic relationships.

claim: The monophyletic group Eucynodontia possessed endothermic-like metabolism based on isotope interpretations.
source: Based on our interpretations, the monophyletic group Eucynodontia (Ruta et al., 2013) (including Cynognathus, Diademodon, an indeterminate cynodont from Lesotho, and extant mammals) possessed endothermic-like metabolism.
evidence: This interpretation is based on isotope data and phylogenetic relationships.

claim: The origin of mammal endothermy occurred within non-Eucynodontia Epicynodontia, between the end-Permian and the earliest Triassic.
source: A parsimonious interpretation would imply rooting the origin of mammal endothermy within non-Eucynodontia Epicynodontia, between the end-Permian and the earliest Triassic.
evidence: This is an inference based on isotope data and phylogenetic parsimony.

claim: The closest sampled relative of Eucynodontia, the late Permian basal cynodont (SAM-PK-K05339), was probably ectothermic.
source: According to our results, the closest sampled relative of Eucynodontia, the late Permian basal cynodont (SAM-PK-K05339), was probably ectothermic.
evidence: This interpretation is based on isotope data from the study.

claim: The origin of mammal endothermy could have taken place among 'intermediate' groups belonging to the Epicynodontia such as Cynosaurus or Thrinaxodon.
source: Therefore the origin of mammal endothermy could have taken place among 'intermediate' groups belonging to the Epicynodontia (such as Cynosaurus from the latest Permian or Thrinaxodon from the Early Triassic of South Africa) that have in the past been considered to have been endothermic, based on anatomical features (Hillenius and Ruben, 2004; Benoit et al., 2015, 2016a).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on isotope data, phylogenetic relationships, and citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Endothermic-like body temperature regulations seem to have originated independently within the L+K and Epicynodontia clades during the late Permian (Lopingian).
source: In agreement with recent phylogenies (Kemp, 2012; Ruta et al., 2013), endothermic-like body temperature regulations seem to root sometime during the late Permian (Lopingian) independently within the L+K and Epicynodontia clades, the latter being at the origin of mammal endothermy.
evidence: This is an inference based on isotope data, phylogenetic relationships, and citations.

claim: An alternative hypothesis considers that both the L+K and Epicynodontia clades possessed a homologous endothermy inherited from their direct common ancestors, the basal Neotherapsida.
source: An alternative hypothesis considers that both the L+K and Epicynodontia clades possessed a homologous endothermy inherited from their direct common ancestors, the basal Neotherapsida (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a speculative alternative interpretation based on phylogenetic relationships shown in Figure 4.

claim: The alternative hypothesis suggests that biochemical and physiological mechanisms enabling mammal endothermy appeared at the base of the neotherapsids during the middle Permian.
source: This suggests that biochemical and physiological mechanisms enabling mammal endothermy, appeared at the base of the neotherapsids during the middle Permian, which is a conclusion recently published based on the paleohistology of some dicynodonts (Olivier et al., 2017).
evidence: This alternative hypothesis is supported by citation to Olivier et al., 2017.

claim: The absence of an endothermic signal in the sampled Permian therapsids could be due to endothermy being only seasonal.
source: In our case, the absence of an endothermic signal in the sampled Permian therapsids could be due to an endothermy being only seasonal, linked to the presence of a cold season or to the reproduction period (as observed today in some reptile species; Tattersall et al., 2016), which would not be visible in a bulk signal.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation to Tattersall et al., 2016.

claim: Global and regional palaeoclimate reconstructions show a cooling trend toward the end-Permian, followed by an abrupt and intense warming at the Permian-Triassic Boundary.
source: Global and regional palaeoclimate reconstructions show a cooling trend toward the end-Permian, followed by an abrupt and intense warming at the Permian-Triassic Boundary (Chen et al., 2013; Rey et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2013 and Rey et al., 2016.

claim: Most of the therapsid clades which survived the end-Permian mass extinction were supposedly endothermic.
source: Interestingly, most of the therapsid clades which survived the end-Permian mass extinction were supposedly endothermic.
evidence: This is an inference based on the isotope interpretations presented in the study.

claim: Climatic fluctuations may have acted as selective pressures which favoured or 'activated' elevated thermometabolic capabilities within therapsids.
source: It thus appears that climatic fluctuations may have acted as selective pressures which favoured or 'activated' elevated thermometabolic capabilities within therapsids, at the origins of mammal endothermy.
evidence: This is a speculative inference connecting climate data with the evolution of endothermy.

claim: According to a recent palaeohistology study, Early Triassic therapsids such as Lystrosaurus, therocephalians and cynodonts had a high growth rate allowing them to reach reproductive maturity within a few seasons.
source: According to a recent palaeohistology study (Botha-Brink et al., 2016), Early Triassic therapsids, such as Lystrosaurus or even therocephalians and cynodonts, had a high growth rate allowing them to reach reproductive maturity within a few seasons and compensate their shortened life expectancies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Botha-Brink et al., 2016.

claim: High growth rate adaptation might have enabled certain therapsids to survive the intense climatic change and conquer newly vacant niches.
source: This adaptation might have enabled certain therapsids to survive the intense climatic change of that time and conquer the newly vacant niches.
evidence: This is a speculative inference connecting growth rate data with survival during climate change.

claim: Nineteen new fossil apatite samples were analysed to determine stable oxygen isotope compositions of apatite phosphate and carbonate.
source: Nineteen new fossil apatite samples were analysed to determine stable oxygen isotope compositions of apatite phosphate and carbonate, along with 89 samples for which oxygen isotope compositions have already been published (Rey et al., 2016; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the data collection for the study.

claim: The sample total comprises 41 teeth and 65 bones of 90 individual tetrapods from Permian and Triassic deposits of South Africa, Lesotho, Morocco and China.
source: This sample total comprises 41 teeth and 65 bones of 90 individual tetrapods (Therapsida, Archosauriformes, Parareptilia and Stereospondyli) recovered from Permian and Triassic deposits of South Africa, Lesotho, Morocco and China.
evidence: This describes the sample composition for the study.

claim: The Permo-Triassic boundary is now considered to be at 251.90 ± 0.02 Ma.
source: All the sample localities are correlated to the marine biostratigraphic stages using the absolute ages accepted by the International Commission on Stratigraphy (Cohen et al., 2013); updated 12/2016), with the Permo-Triassic and Guadalupian-Lopingian boundaries now respectively considered to be at 251.90 ± 0.02 Ma (Burgess et al., 2014) and 259.1 ± 0.5 (Zhong et al., 2014) Ma.
evidence: This is established geochronological knowledge supported by citation to Burgess et al., 2014.

claim: The Guadalupian-Lopingian boundary is now considered to be at 259.1 ± 0.5 Ma.
source: All the sample localities are correlated to the marine biostratigraphic stages using the absolute ages accepted by the International Commission on Stratigraphy (Cohen et al., 2013); updated 12/2016), with the Permo-Triassic and Guadalupian-Lopingian boundaries now respectively considered to be at 251.90 ± 0.02 Ma (Burgess et al., 2014) and 259.1 ± 0.5 (Zhong et al., 2014) Ma.
evidence: This is established geochronological knowledge supported by citation to Zhong et al., 2014.

claim: Bone and tooth dentine are more porous than enamel with small and less densely inter-grown apatite crystals.
source: Analysed materials consist of bone or tooth dentine, which is more porous than enamel with small and less densely inter-grown apatite crystals
evidence: This is established knowledge about bone and tooth microstructure.

claim: Samples that have δ18Oc-δ18Op differences higher than 14.7‰ are considered doubtful as regards potential diagenetic alteration.
source: Samples that have δ18Oc-δ18Op differences higher than 14.7‰ are considered doubtful as regards potential diagenetic alteration (see text).
evidence: This is a methodological criterion established in the study, shown in Figure 5.

claim: For carbonate contents (wt%) higher than 13.4%, the δ18Oc values are considered to be inherited from inorganic diagenetic processes.
source: For carbonate contents (wt%) higher than 13.4%, the δ18Oc values are considered to be inherited from inorganic diagenetic processes.
evidence: This is a methodological criterion established in the study, shown in Figure 5.

claim: A high difference between δ18Oc and δ18Op is interpreted as the result of microbially-mediated alteration of the apatite phosphate or too high δ18Oc values resulting from the addition of inorganic carbonate or isotopic exchange with an external source of inorganic carbon.
source: A high difference between δ18Oc and δ18Op is interpreted as the result of a microbially-mediated alteration of the apatite phosphate or too high δ18Oc values resulting from the addition of inorganic carbonate or isotopic exchange with an external source of inorganic carbon.
evidence: This is an interpretation of diagenetic processes based on isotope data shown in Figure 5.
